profile.reading:
Iron Mountain Incorporated (NYSE: IRM) is a publicly traded REIT headquartered in Portsmouth, New Hampshire, whose core business is physical and digital records management; its data center division was built substantially through a January 2018 acquisition of IO Data Centers. Per the operator's own site, Iron Mountain's global data center portfolio spans more than 30 locations across three continents totaling roughly 1.4 GW of capacity.

This facility, AZS-1, sits on a 4.5-acre campus at 8521 E Princess Drive in Scottsdale, Arizona, confirmed against the operator's own Scottsdale location page. It is a distinct campus from Iron Mountain's larger, roughly 39-acre Phoenix campus (AZP-1, AZP-2, and a third building, AZP-3, which the operator's own site lists but which is not separately tracked as a row in this registry); the two campuses are linked by a 100 Gbps dark-fiber ring. AZS-1 offers 121,000 square feet across four raised-floor data halls on 36-inch raised flooring, with 5.8 MW of IT capacity currently operational and stated room to expand to 9.6 MW. The operator describes full 2N redundant power, densities up to 32 kW per cabinet, more than 16 on-site network providers, 100% matched renewable power, and a PUE as low as 1.2.

Iron Mountain's 2018 acquisition of IO Data Centers added four colocation facilities in New Jersey, Ohio, and two in Arizona, per Wikipedia's account of the deal; this registry has not found a primary source specifying whether AZS-1 itself was one of the two acquired Arizona sites or a later, ground-up Iron Mountain build, so that lineage is left unconfirmed rather than assumed either way. No year-opened figure or independently verified Uptime Institute tier certificate was located for this building in sourcing to date.

Iron Mountain trades on the New York Stock Exchange under ticker IRM and files with the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission under CIK 0001020569, structured as a real estate investment trust. Records management remains the company's larger, founding business line by facility count; the data center segment is reported separately in Iron Mountain's public filings as a smaller but faster-growing division. Metro Phoenix and Scottsdale have grown into one of the largest US data center markets outside the traditional Northern Virginia and Dallas hubs, drawing operators in part on lower land costs and a large regional power grid footprint.
profile.capacity_note: Operator states 5.8 MW currently operational, expandable to 9.6 MW. A separate operator reference described the facility as "Tier III Certified," but this was not seen in a clearly-labeled, dated Uptime Institute certificate form; treated as an operator self-description rather than a confirmed third-party Uptime certification.

reading.body:
Iron Mountain Data Centers AZS-1 publishes no power, IT load, or cooling capacity, making it impossible to assess whether this Scottsdale facility constrains AI infrastructure decisions.

Arizona operates 56 mapped data centers. Only four of them publish power specifications, totaling 512 MW combined. AZS-1 does not appear in that disclosed total. The facility sits 22 kilometers north of Iron Mountain's Phoenix campus, suggesting operational integration with the state's mapped infrastructure, yet remains invisible in Arizona's published capacity footprint.

The absence of published specifications reflects a structural gap in infrastructure visibility. Either AZS-1 is not marketed for hyperscale AI workloads, or Iron Mountain has chosen not to disclose its capacity for this location. Without these numbers, the facility cannot be ranked among sites that matter to AI scaling decisions, and cannot be evaluated as a constraint on compute deployment.

This data does not indicate whether AZS-1 is powered, how much power it consumes, or what workloads it serves. It documents only the boundary of what is known: a facility exists, its location is mapped, and its specifications remain private.
